He chose Friday, August 17, for his appearance and devoted most of the day to inspecting his wardrobe. Eventually he settled on a broad, drooping hat with a red feather, a burial shroud frilled at the neck and wrists, and a rusty dagger. Toward evening a fierce rainstorm began, with winds strong enough to shake and rattle every door and window in the old house. It was precisely the weather he enjoyed. His strategy was as follows. He would slip quietly into Washington Otis's room, gibber at him from the end of the bed, and stab himself in the throat three times to slow musical accompaniment. He particularly resented Washington, knowing perfectly well that he was responsible for repeatedly removing the celebrated Canterville bloodstain with Pinkerton's Paragon Detergent. Once he had terrified the reckless, foolhardy young man into helplessness, he would move on to the bedroom of the United States Minister and his wife. There he would lay a cold, damp hand on Mrs. Otis's forehead while hissing the dreadful secrets of the burial vault into her shaking husband's ear. He had not entirely decided what to do about little Virginia. She was pretty and gentle and had never offended him. A handful of hollow groans from her wardrobe would surely be enough; if they failed to wake her, he could clutch at her bedspread with twitching, palsied fingers. As for the twins, he was determined to teach them a lesson. Naturally, he would begin by sitting on their chests to create the suffocating sensation of a nightmare. Since their beds stood close together, he would then position himself between them as a green, ice-cold corpse until terror paralyzed them. Finally, throwing off his shroud, he would crawl about the room with bleached white bones and a single rolling eyeball, performing “Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide's Skeleton.” He had achieved impressive results with this role on several occasions and considered it every bit as good as his celebrated “Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.”

At ten thirty he heard the family retiring for the night. For a while the twins disturbed him with shrieks of laughter; evidently they were entertaining themselves before bed with the carefree high spirits of schoolboys. By eleven fifteen, though, the house had fallen silent, and as midnight struck, he ventured out. An owl beat against the windowpanes, a raven croaked in the old yew tree, and the wind drifted around the house, moaning like a lost soul. But the Otis family slept on, unaware of the fate awaiting them, and above the rain and storm he could clearly hear the United States Minister's steady snores.

“I hope I'll soon have the pleasure of introducing you to my son,” Mr. Weston said.

Mrs. Elton, quite prepared to interpret this hope as a special compliment to herself, gave him a most gracious smile.

“I assume you've heard of a certain Frank Churchill,” he continued, “and know that he's my son, although we don't share a surname.”

“Oh, yes! I shall be delighted to meet him. I'm sure Mr. Elton will call on him at the first opportunity, and we shall both be very pleased to welcome him to the Vicarage.”

“That's very kind of you. Frank will be delighted, I'm sure. He's coming to London next week, perhaps sooner. A letter arrived today to tell us. I came across the letters while I was out this morning, and when I recognized my son's handwriting I took the liberty of opening it—though it wasn't addressed to me, but to Mrs. Weston. She's the one he mainly writes to, I assure you. I hardly ever receive a letter.”

“So you actually opened a letter addressed to her! Oh, Mr. Weston,” she said, with an affected laugh, “I must object to that. What a dangerous precedent! Please don't let your neighbors follow your example. Honestly, if that's what I have to look forward to, we married women must start standing up for ourselves! Oh, Mr. Weston, I would never have thought it of you!”

“Yes, we're terrible fellows, we men. You must look out for yourself, Mrs. Elton. The letter tells us—it's a short one, written in a hurry, just to let us know—that they're all coming to London straightaway, because of Mrs. Churchill. She's been unwell all winter and thinks Enscombe is too cold for her. So they're all moving south without delay.”

“Really! From Yorkshire, I think. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes. They're about a hundred and ninety miles from London. Quite a journey.”

“Yes, indeed, a very considerable one. Sixty-five miles farther than Maple Grove is from London. But what does distance matter, Mr. Weston, to people with large fortunes? You'd be astonished at how my brother, Mr. Suckling, sometimes dashes about. You'll scarcely believe it, but in a single week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back twice, with four horses.”

“The difficulty with the distance from Enscombe,” Mr. Weston replied, “is that Mrs. Churchill, _as we understand it_, hasn't been able to get off the sofa for an entire week. In Frank's last letter, he said she'd complained of being too weak to walk to her conservatory unless she had both his arm and his uncle's to support her!”

The following day the ghost felt exceedingly feeble and weary. The dreadful agitation of the preceding four weeks was beginning to tell upon him. His nerves were utterly wrecked, and the faintest sound made him jump. For five days he remained in his room, finally resolving to abandon the matter of the blood-stain on the library floor. If the Otises had no wish for it, plainly they were unworthy of it. They were manifestly creatures of a low and material order, wholly unable to esteem the symbolic significance of phenomena perceived by the senses. Spectral appearances and the formation of astral bodies were, of course, another matter altogether, and not really within his discretion. He had a sacred obligation to show himself in the passage every week and to gibber at the great oriel window upon the first and third Wednesday of each month; he could discover no honourable means of avoiding those responsibilities. His life, admittedly, had been a very wicked one; on the other hand, in every supernatural concern he was scrupulously dutiful. Accordingly, on the next three Saturdays he made his customary passage along the corridor between twelve and three, using every precaution to avoid detection by eye or ear. He took off his boots, stepped as softly as he could on the ancient worm-eaten planks, put on a great cloak of black velvet, and carefully applied the Rising Sun Lubricator to his chains. I must confess that he overcame considerable resistance within himself before accepting this last defensive measure. Nevertheless, one evening while the family dined, he stole into Mr. Otis's bedchamber and took away the bottle. At first he suffered some humiliation, but subsequently had the sense to perceive the invention's many merits, and found that it answered his needs to some extent. Yet all these precautions failed to secure him peace. Strings were constantly drawn across the passage, tripping him in the darkness; and once, arrayed as “Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,” he suffered a serious tumble after stepping upon a slide of butter laid by the twins between the Tapestry Chamber doorway and the head of the oak stairs. This latest indignity provoked such fury that he decided upon one last attempt to vindicate his dignity and station, resolving to visit the impudent young Etonians the following night as his renowned “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.”

More than seventy years had passed since he last assumed that disguise; indeed, he had not worn it since it terrified the lovely Lady Barbara Modish into abruptly ending her engagement to the present Lord Canterville's grandfather and eloping to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton. She declared that nothing on earth could persuade her to marry into a family which permitted so appalling a spectre to pace its terrace in the twilight.
